message.content:
Below you’ll find a “tool‑box” of ways—command line utilities, scripts, and even programmatic interfaces—to pull **detailed information** about a specific network interface on most common platforms: | Platform | Tool(s) | What it gives you | Typical usage | |----------|---------|-------------------|---------------| | **Linux / Unix** | `ip link show dev eth0`
`ip addr show dev eth0`
`cat /sys/class/net/eth0/*`
`ethtool eth0`
`lshw -class network -short` | • Interface state (UP/DOWN)
• MTU
• Speed & duplex
• Driver name + firmware
• MAC address
• Tx/Rx counters
• Link statistics (errors, collisions) | ```bash\nip link show dev eth0 # basic flags, speed, mtu\nip addr show dev eth0 # IPv4/IPv6 addresses, broadcast, scope\nsudo ethtool eth0 # driver, supported speeds, autonegotiation\ncat /sys/class/net/eth0/address # MAC address\n``` | | **macOS** | `ifconfig en0`
`netstat -i en0`
`networksetup -listallhardwareports` | Same set of data – plus hardware port mapping (e.g., Wi‑Fi vs Ethernet) | ```bash\nifconfig en0 # all low‑level config\nnetstat -i en0 # packet stats per interface\n``` | **Windows** | PowerShell cmdlets:
`Get-NetIPConfiguration -InterfaceAlias Ethernet1`
`Get-NetAdapterStatistics -Name Ethernet1`
`Get-NetAdapterAdvancedProperty -Name Ethernet1` | • IP configuration (static/dhcp)
• Adapter performance counters
• Advanced properties (speed, duplex, flow control) | ```powershell\nGet-NetIPAddress -InterfaceAlias Ethernet1\nGet-NetAdapterStatistics -Name Ethernet1\n``` | **Network Devices (Cisco IOS)** | CLI:
`show interface GigabitEthernet0/1`
`display interface GigabitEthernet0/1` (Huawei) | • Operational status
• Physical layer errors
• Port description
• VLAN membership
• QoS settings | ```cisco-cli\nshow interface Gi0/1\n``` | **Programmable Interfaces** | *RESTCONF* (RFC8040): `/restconf/data/interfaces/interface=GigabitEthernet0%2F1`
*SNMP*: OIDs under IF-MIB::ifTable (e.g., `IF-MIB::ifDescr`) | Allows automated collection of the same metrics over the network. Useful for monitoring systems or inventory databases. | Example SNMP walk: `snmpwalk -v2c -c public host.ifDescr` | --- ### Step‑by‑Step Guide (Linux example) Let’s say we’re interested in interface `ens33`. Here’s a quick walkthrough: 1. **Basic Status** ```bash $ ip link show ens33 5: ens33: mtu 1500 qdisc mq state UP mode DEFAULT group default qlen 1000 link/ether aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff ``` *Flags:* - `UP`: Interface administratively up. - `LOWER_UP`: Carrier detected at physical level. 2. **Address Configuration** ```bash $ ip addr show ens33 inet 192.168.10.42/24 brd 192.168.10.255 scope global dynamic ens33 valid_lft 86399sec preferred_lft 86399sec inet6 fe80::aabb:ccff:fedd:eefb/64 scope link ``` Shows both IPv4 and IPv6 assignments, lease times, etc. 3. **Driver & Hardware Details** ```bash $ sudo lspci -nnk | grep -A2 -E "(Eth|Net)" 02:00.0 Network controller [0200]: Intel Corporation I350 Gigabit Network Connection [8086:a123] (rev 01) Subsystem: Dell Inc. I350 Gigabit Network Connection [1028:b7f9] Kernel driver in use: e1000e Kernel modules: igb ``` 4. **Link Layer Stats** ```bash $ cat /sys/class/net/ens33/statistics/rx_packets 12567890 $ cat /sys/class/net/ens33/statistics/multicast 34567 ``` 5. **Speed & Duplex** ```bash $ sudo ethtool ens33 Settings for ens33: Supported ports: [ TP ] Supported modes: 10baseT/Half 10baseT/Full 100baseT/Half 100baseT/Full 1000baseT/Full Supports auto-negotiation: yes Advertised link partner ability: 10baseT/Half 10baseT/Full 100baseT/Half 100baseT/Full 1000baseT/Full Link detected: yes Current speed: 1000Mb/s Full-duplex: Yes Auto-negotiation: On ``` 6. **Error Counters** ```bash $ sudo ethtool -S ens33 | grep error rx_errors : 0 tx_errors : 0 collisions : 0 ``` --- ### Using SNMP to Pull the Same Data Programmatically If you prefer automation, here’s a minimal example using Net-SNMP's `snmpwalk`: ```bash $ snmpwalk -v2c -c community_string hostname \ .1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.1 | grep -n ens33 ``` This walks the IF-MIB table and filters out rows matching your target interface. You can then map other OIDs (e.g., `.1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.16` for transmitted octets). For more advanced scenarios, consider writing a small script in Python using libraries like `pysnmp` or `ncclient` (for NETCONF) to fetch and parse the values into structured objects. --- #### Quick Reference Cheat Sheet | Metric | Command | Notes | |--------|---------|-------| | MAC Address | `cat /sys/class/net//address` | Raw hex | | IP Addresses | `ip addr show ` | Includes DHCP lease time | | MTU | `cat /sys/class/net//mtu` | Usually 1500 unless jumbo frames enabled | | Speed | `ethtool | grep Speed` | Requires root | | Errors | `ethtool -S | grep error` | Good health indicator | | Traffic Counters | `/sys/class/net//statistics/{rx_bytes,tx_bytes}` | Use `watch -n1` for live updates | | Vendor Info | `udevadm info --query=property --name=` | Gives PCI vendor ID | Feel free to let me know which platform or environment you’re working in, and I can tailor the commands further!
